capabilities.name: banner_and_product_grab
capabilities.description: Read the mandatory +OK greeting (RFC 1939 §4), pull product/version (Dovecot/Courier/Cyrus/qpopper/Exchange) so it feeds the offline CVE DB.
capabilities.notes: svcdetect already extracts Dovecot/Courier/Cyrus via parse_product_version — reuse that same regex table.

capabilities.name: apop_timestamp_disclosure
capabilities.description: Any APOP-capable server emits a <processid.timestamp@hostname> token in the greeting (RFC 1939 §7) — the hostname suffix leaks internal FQDN/domain and is a first-class known_hostnames/known_domains input.

capabilities.name: capa_enumeration
capabilities.description: Issue CAPA (RFC 2449) to enumerate advertised features — STLS, SASL, USER, PIPELINING, TOP, UIDL, LOGIN-DELAY, EXPIRE, RESP-CODES, IMPLEMENTATION — driving every downstream decision.

capabilities.name: implementation_disclosure
capabilities.description: The IMPLEMENTATION capability (RFC 2449 §6.9) explicitly returns a product/version string that supplements the greeting banner and often gives a version when the banner does not.

capabilities.name: stls_missing_on_110
capabilities.description: Absence of the STLS capability on port 110 (RFC 2595) means the AUTHORIZATION phase can only run in cleartext — a definite cleartext-credential exposure independent of any successful auth.

capabilities.name: user_enum_differential
capabilities.description: Send USER <name> for a known-bad and a known-good name (or known_users feed) and diff the +OK/-ERR response and latency — RFC 1939 §5 lets servers reject USER before PASS, which is the classic username oracle (Dovecot user_query, Exchange 'user unknown').

capabilities.name: sasl_mechanism_enum
capabilities.description: Issue AUTH with no argument (RFC 1734/5034) to list SASL mechanisms — PLAIN/LOGIN/CRAM-MD5/DIGEST-MD5/SCRAM-SHA-*/NTLM/GSSAPI — so the runbook picks the right offline-crackable or relayable path.

capabilities.name: cleartext_auth_accepted
capabilities.description: USER/PASS or AUTH PLAIN/LOGIN accepted before STLS is negotiated — proves credentials cross the wire in cleartext and are sniffable.

capabilities.name: ntlm_auth_type2_leak
capabilities.description: Where AUTH NTLM is advertised, send a Type-1 blob and decode the returned Type-2 challenge — it discloses NetBIOS name, DNS hostname, DNS domain, forest DNS name (same primitive smtp NTLM info exploits) — huge feed into known_hostnames/known_domains.

capabilities.name: implicit_tls_cert_inspect
capabilities.description: On 995 (implicit TLS, RFC 8314) grab the server certificate — CN/SANs feed known_hostnames and known_domains, expiry/self-signed status becomes a finding.

capabilities.name: apop_offline_crack_chain
capabilities.description: APOP responses are md5(timestamp || password); a captured or replayed APOP transcript (timestamp from the greeting + APOP <user> <digest>) is offline-crackable — hashcat mode 11500 style workflow, feeds known_hashes/relay-adjacent surface.

capabilities.name: credentialed_mailbox_dump
capabilities.description: With a valid login (from cred-quickconnect / known_users + spray), STAT/LIST/UIDL/TOP/RETR to prove read access and pull message headers (From/To/Received) — each Received header seeds known_hostnames and known_domains, each From/To seeds known_users.

capabilities.name: known_cve_by_banner
capabilities.description: Map the extracted product/version to POP3-specific pre-auth CVEs (Dovecot CVE-2019-11500 out-of-bounds write, CVE-2020-12100 RCE, Cyrus SASL memcached, qpopper 4.0.x) — critical-severity findings without touching auth.

capabilities.name: login_delay_aware_spray
capabilities.description: Time-boxed password spray against known_users; LOGIN-DELAY from CAPA (RFC 2449 §6.5) is honoured so we don't self-DOS or trip lockouts. One password / many users, then one user / small list.

capabilities.name: auth_downgrade_detection
capabilities.description: After STLS negotiate, re-issue CAPA — if the plaintext mechanism set is still advertised (i.e. server never drops PLAIN/LOGIN inside TLS) that is a hardening finding; also detect servers where STLS is offered but broken (RFC 2595 §4).

cross_service_wire_candidates: known_hostnames <- APOP greeting timestamp <pid.time@HOST> (RFC 1939 §7): the @HOST suffix is often an internal FQDN not otherwise discovered.
known_hostnames + known_domains <- POP3S (995) TLS certificate CN and Subject Alternative Names.

known_hostnames + known_domains <- NTLM Type-2 challenge Target Info AV_PAIRs (MsvAvNbComputerName, MsvAvDnsComputerName, MsvAvDnsDomainName, MsvAvDnsTreeName) — same primitive already harvested from SMTP NTLM info.
known_users <- valid usernames confirmed by USER-command differential (RFC 1939 §5) or by successful spray, before any real password is known.
known_users + known_domains <- credentialed RETR of message headers: every From:/To:/Cc:/Received-by mailbox seeds users@domain across the whole environment.

known_hashes (new sub-surface: apop_challenges) <- captured/replayed APOP timestamps and APOP <user> <digest> lines are offline-crackable as md5(challenge||password); feeds hashcat -m 11500-style workflow.
relay_targets (new sub-surface: ntlm_endpoints) <- any POP3 port advertising AUTH NTLM is a candidate for NTLM relay targeting alongside SMB/LDAP/HTTP/SMTP/IMAP.
cred_quickconnect <- POP3 is a fast, low-noise verify surface for a captured mailbox credential (a single AUTH PLAIN round-trip proves it) — should register alongside SMTP submission and IMAP.

existing_coverage.notes: svcdetect.py L95 signature-matches '+OK' to service 'pop3'; parse_product_version() at L134-135 pulls Dovecot/Courier/Cyrus product+version from the banner (feeds the offline CVE DB). serviceenum.py maps pop3/pop3s/imap/imaps names AND ports 110/143/993/995 to a shared 'pop-imap' bash script under scripts/recce-service.sh. core/scanner.py L238 acknowledges the nmap script names 'pop3-capabilities' and 'pop3-ntlm-info' in NSE runs. There is NO dedicated recce/services/pop3.py module — no CAPA parser, no STLS/user-enum/AUTH-mech probe, no SASL / NTLM info extractor, no finding builder, no runbook, no analyze() entry point. This is the gap this punch list is planning.

recommended_findings.title: POP3 accepts USER/PASS in cleartext (no STLS)
POP3 STLS not advertised on port 110
POP3 username enumeration via differential USER response
POP3 AUTH NTLM leaks NetBIOS/DNS names (Type-2 challenge)
POP3 APOP timestamp discloses internal hostname/domain
POP3 SASL PLAIN/LOGIN still offered inside TLS (no downgrade lockout)
POP3 weak/reused credentials confirmed by spray
POP3S (995) certificate is self-signed / expired / mismatched

recommended_hashcat_modes.description: APOP challenge/response — md5($challenge.$pass) family; the APOP timestamp is the challenge, the APOP <digest> is the response.
If credentialed RETR pulls a Dovecot passwd-file or a /etc/shadow-like backup out of a mailbox attachment, md5crypt (Dovecot's default MD5-CRYPT scheme) is directly crackable.

implementation_notes: Model the module on recce/services/ftp.py (text-banner, control-channel probe, finding_builder from svccommon) and on recce/services/smtp.py where the NTLM Type-2 info leak, CAPA-style enumeration, and STARTTLS/STLS posture are basically the same primitives — reuse svccommon.finding_builder and svcprobe.iter_probe. Stdlib only (poplib exists but is thin; a raw socket + line reader is what ftp.py uses and matches the airgap constraint). Send commands in the RFC 1939 order — CAPA first (never assume it exists; some ancient qpopper builds -ERR it), then USER for a known-bad, then STLS if advertised, then AUTH. Time every USER response and diff — LOGIN-DELAY from CAPA must be respected so the probe does not self-throttle or lock accounts. On 995 wrap the socket in ssl.create_default_context(check_hostname=False) and grab getpeercert(binary_form=True) for cert facts. Route valid usernames + captured APOP transcripts into the shared cross-service surfaces described above (known_users, known_hostnames, apop_challenges) via the same wire code smtp/ldap use. Do NOT collide with the existing pop-imap bash script — the Python module owns findings + programmatic probes; the bash script stays as the tester-facing 'what do I type here' helper (serviceenum still points at it).
summary: POP3 (RFC 1939) is a plaintext line-based mailbox-retrieval protocol on 110/tcp, with implicit TLS on 995/tcp (RFC 8314) and opportunistic STLS on 110 (RFC 2595); capability discovery is via CAPA (RFC 2449) and authentication is USER/PASS, APOP (RFC 1939 §7), or SASL AUTH (RFC 1734/5034). What an attacker cares about: (1) the mandatory +OK greeting and the CAPA/IMPLEMENTATION strings pin the product/version for CVE mapping; (2) APOP timestamps leak internal hostnames/domains and are offline-crackable when a transcript is captured; (3) USER-before-PASS is a textbook username enumeration oracle; (4) STLS-not-advertised on 110 is definitive cleartext-credential exposure; (5) AUTH NTLM leaks NetBIOS/DNS names in the Type-2 challenge (same primitive we already harvest from SMTP); (6) with a valid credential, mailbox headers seed a massive users/hostnames/domains graph. recce already recognises the port (svcdetect signature-matches +OK and parse_product_version pulls Dovecot/Courier/Cyrus banners) and hands the tester a shared pop-imap bash script, but there is no dedicated recce/services/pop3.py — no CAPA parser, no STLS/user-enum/SASL/NTLM-info probe, no finding builder, no runbook, no cross-service wire — so this service currently contributes nothing to the vulnerability sheet or to the shared known_* surfaces. The punch list below closes that gap.
